title: Ursitoare, the Weavers of Destiny
summary: Three fate-weaving spirits who appear at a child's birth to determine the course of its life, found in Moldovan and Romanian tradition.
full_text:
On the third night after a child is born, the doors of Moldovan homes are left unlocked. Candles burn in every window. A loaf of bread and a cup of wine are placed on a clean white cloth near the cradle. This is for the Ursitoare, the three weavers of destiny who visit every newborn child.

The Ursitoare are sisters. The first is young and beautiful, her hands quick and light. The second is middle-aged, her face lined with wisdom. The third is ancient, her fingers gnarled, her eyes deep as wells. They come at midnight, silent as shadows, and stand around the cradle. Each holds a spindle of thread. The first spins the thread of the child's life, the second measures it, and the third cuts it. The length of the thread determines how long the child will live. The quality of the spinning determines his fortune.

A family in the village of Soroca once prepared a lavish welcome for the Ursitoare, covering the table with honey cakes and sweet wine. The youngest sister smiled and spun a thread of gold. The child grew up to be a great scholar, beloved and prosperous. But a miserly farmer named Ion left nothing for the Ursitoare, not even a crumb of bread. The eldest sister, angered by his greed, knotted the thread three times. The child grew up healthy but faced obstacle after obstacle, each knot a trial that nearly broke him.

The Ursitoare cannot be bribed, but they appreciate gratitude. A small offering, a clean room, a heartfelt prayer, these incline them toward kindness. To this day, Moldovan grandmothers prepare for the Ursitoare on the third night, whispering old prayers and hoping that the weavers of destiny will be generous.
moral: How you welcome life shapes the life you welcome.

title: Strigoi, the Undead of the Carpathians
summary: Restless spirits of the dead who rise from their graves to plague the living, the Strigoi are among the most feared creatures in Moldovan folklore.
full_text:
In the hills of Moldova, where the Carpathian foothills cast long shadows and the mist clings to the graveyards, the dead do not always stay dead. The Strigoi are the restless ones, the souls who cannot find peace. They rise from their graves at night, their bodies intact but their eyes hollow and burning with a light that is not of this world.

A person becomes a Strigoi for many reasons. A life lived in sin. A death without proper rites. A grave dug in unholy ground. Sometimes a man becomes a Strigoi simply because he was born with a caul over his face or because he was the seventh son of a seventh son. The signs are unmistakable: the body does not decay, the grave remains warm to the touch, and on the night of the full moon, the earth above the coffin is disturbed.

The Strigoi do not merely haunt. They feed. They drain the life from cattle, the strength from children, the breath from sleeping adults. A village plagued by a Strigoi would find its wells running dry, its crops failing, its people wasting away. The only cure was to open the grave, drive a stake through the heart, and place a clove of garlic in the mouth. Sometimes a sprig of wild rose was laid across the chest to pin the soul to the earth.

An old priest in Orhei told of a Strigoi who was once a kind man, a baker beloved by all. But he died of a broken heart after his betrothed married another. His ghost returned every night to stand outside her window, sighing. He harmed no one, but his presence drained the life from the village. The priest persuaded the woman to place a loaf of bread on the grave, a symbol of forgiveness. The Strigoi never rose again.
moral: Unresolved love and unfinished business bind the soul to the world.

title: Iele, the Dancing Spirits of the Meadow
summary: Beautiful but dangerous fairy spirits who dance in moonlit meadows, luring travelers to join their fatal dance.
full_text:
When the moon is full and the summer air is warm, there are places in the Moldovan countryside where the grass grows in perfect circles, greener than the rest. These are the rings of the Iele, the dancing spirits of the meadow. The Iele appear as young women of impossible beauty, dressed in white with flowers in their hair. They dance in a circle, their feet never touching the ground, their voices blending into a melody sweeter than any human song.

To see the Iele is to be enchanted. Their dance draws the eye, their song pulls at the heart. A man who watches them from a distance may find himself walking toward them without meaning to. If he joins their circle, he will dance until dawn, his feet bleeding, his lungs burning, his mind emptied of all thought. When the sun rises, the Iele vanish, and the man is left alone in the field, exhausted and broken. He will never be the same. Some never speak again. Others waste away, dreaming always of the dance.

A shepherd named Andrei once came upon the Iele in a meadow near the Prut River. He was wise enough to know what they were. He did not approach. He sat at the edge of the forest, facing away from them, and played a slow song on his flute. The Iele stopped dancing and listened. Their queen approached him and said, 'You are the first who did not try to join us.' Andrei replied, 'A dance that ends in death is no dance at all.' The Iele queen laughed and vanished. Andrei lived to be an old man, and his flocks never strayed.

To this day, Moldovan peasants avoid circular patches of dark green grass. They know the Iele are still dancing there, waiting for someone to join the circle.
moral: Not all beauty is meant to be touched; some things are only safe to admire from afar.

title: Zmeu, the Dragon of Moldovan Skies
summary: A great dragon-like creature with three heads that terrorizes the Moldovan countryside, often serving as the ultimate test of a hero's courage.
full_text:
In the oldest stories of Moldova, there is a creature that dwarfs all others. The Zmeu is a dragon of terrifying power, with three heads, scales like iron, and wings that blot out the sun. He lives in the highest mountains, in a castle of black stone surrounded by rivers of fire. His breath is poison, his roar shakes the earth, and his hunger is never satisfied.

The Zmeu does not devour cattle or burn villages, though he could if he wished. His desire is for something more precious: the most beautiful maiden in the kingdom. He would fly down from his mountain, snatch her from her home, and carry her to his castle. There she would remain, a prisoner of the dragon, until a hero brave enough to face the Zmeu arrived.

The hero was always a young man, poor but pure of heart. He would walk for days, cross the river of fire, and climb the black mountain. The Zmeu would meet him at the gate and challenge him. The battle lasted three days and three nights. The hero would cut off one head, then another, and finally the third. With each head, the Zmeu grew weaker, until at last he fell. The hero would free the maiden, and they would marry and rule wisely.

A version of the tale from the Codru region tells of a hero named Ionutz who defeated the Zmeu not with a sword but with kindness. He offered the dragon bread and salt, symbols of hospitality. The Zmeu, confused and hungry, accepted. And Ionutz said, 'You are lonely, not evil. Come down from the mountain and live among us.' The Zmeu shrunk to the size of a bird and became a messenger between the heavens and the earth. The story is told to children to teach that even monsters can be tamed with compassion.
moral: Sometimes the greatest courage is offered as kindness, not violence.
